_meta.title: Wireless & Physical Proximity
_meta.description: The layer where the network leaves the cable: Wi-Fi attacks, SDR, and short-range credential emulation. Physical access is root access, and radio is physical access at a distance.

techniques.name: WPA/WPA2 Handshake Capture & Offline Crack
techniques.summary: Deauthenticate a client to force a 4-way handshake rekey, capture it passively, then crack the PMK-derived material offline against a wordlist (or against a stolen PMKID - deauth not even required on many APs). PSK networks with human passwords fall; enterprise networks do not (different attack surface).

detection.description: Deauth frame floods (WIDS flags them instantly), handshake capture correlation, PMKID request frames to the AP from foreign MACs; wireless IDS is the entire game here - wired monitoring sees nothing.
mitigations: WPA2-Enterprise/WPA3-SAE instead of PSK wherever humanly possible
Long random PSKs where PSK must remain (20+ chars, no human words)
802.11w management frame protection (makes deauth much harder)

techniques.name: Evil Twin / Rogue AP
techniques.summary: Clone a legitimate SSID on stronger signal; devices auto-associate (and auto-join wins over the real AP). Capture credentials via a cloned captive portal, strip TLS with user help, or simply MITM everything. The captive-portal phishing variant is nearly indistinguishable to untrained users.

detection.description: Same SSID from multiple BSSIDs, sudden signal-strength competition, clients authenticating twice (once to real AP, once to twin), TLS interception alerts from pinned apps, WIDS rogue-AP classification.
mitigations: Certificate validation everywhere (HSTS preload, pinned enterprise apps)
Client-side: enterprise profile with CA pinning (never trust a new cert silently)
User training: verify captive portal legitimacy (look for the specific internal hostname)

techniques.name: SDR Attacks (Signal Replay / Rolling Code)
techniques.summary: Capture and replay RF signals (gate remotes, key fobs, TPMS, some alarm systems) with a $30 RTL-SDR or HackRF; fixed-code protocols replay instantly, rolling-code systems fall to predictive/capture-while-jamming. The physical world's analog of credential replay.

detection.description: Physical-layer anomalies (RF spectrum monitoring is rare outside critical facilities), unexpected unlock events in access logs, jamming complaints (the jam-then-capture signature), rolling-code sync drift (fob stops working - the user reports it).
mitigations: Rolling-code + challenge-response protocols (modern fobs); retire fixed-code devices
Faraday storage for high-value fobs where threat model warrants
Physical access logging + anomaly review (unlock without corresponding badge event)

techniques.name: HID Injection / BadUSB-class Device Attack
techniques.summary: A USB device enumerating as HID keyboard types scripted commands in seconds (Rubber Ducky-class): open a shell, phone home, done. The host cannot distinguish it from a real keyboard by protocol; only behavioral policy catches it. Physical access plus user curiosity equals initial access.

detection.description: HID device insertion followed immediately by Win+R / terminal keystrokes (Sysmon EID 1 with new devices in EID 2001-2003 correlation), keystroke cadence inhumanly fast, devices appearing in USB history on hosts whose users report no insertion.
mitigations: USB device control policy (allowlist vendor/product, block HID where not required)
Lock screens everywhere - the attack needs an unlocked session
User awareness (unfound USB sticks are the delivery mechanism)
Endpoint hardening so one HID payload cannot chain (CLM, ASR, no auto-elevate)
